text:
Everyone is talking about AI replacing developers.

But here's what I think they're missing.

AI won't replace developers who know how to solve problems. It will replace developers who only know how to write code without understanding why they're writing it.

The real skill in 2026 isn't memorizing syntax.
It's asking better questions, understanding systems, and knowing when AI is wrong.

Learn to build, not just to code.

What do you think?

Stop consuming 10 hours of productivity content every week.

Start implementing just ONE idea.

You don't need another video about waking up at 5 AM.
You don't need another productivity app.
You don't need a perfect Notion dashboard.

You need consistency.

Read less about getting better.
Spend more time actually getting better.

That's the difference between looking productive and being productive.

I tested 7 AI tools so you don't have to.

Here's what actually impressed me:

1. ChatGPT - Great for reasoning and brainstorming.
2. Perplexity - Useful for research with sources.
3. NotebookLM - Amazing for understanding documents.
4. Cursor - Speeds up development workflows.
5. Gamma - Creates presentations quickly.
6. Make - Helps automate repetitive workflows.
7. Claude - Strong for writing and coding tasks.

But here's the catch:

Having 20 AI subscriptions won't make you productive.
Knowing how to use 2 tools properly might.

Which AI tool is part of your daily workflow?

Unpopular opinion: Your personal brand is not your follower count.

I've seen creators with 500 followers generate more meaningful opportunities than accounts with 50K followers.

Why?

Because building a personal brand is about trust, not vanity metrics.

Share what you know.
Document what you learn.
Help people solve real problems.
Be consistent even when nobody is watching.

Followers are an outcome.
Value is the strategy.

Agree or disagree?

A simple framework to write better LinkedIn posts:

HOOK → Make people stop scrolling.

STORY → Give them a reason to keep reading.

VALUE → Teach something useful.

TAKEAWAY → Leave them with one memorable idea.

QUESTION → Invite people into the conversation.

You don't need complicated vocabulary or fancy writing.

You need clarity, relatability, and something worth sharing.

Save this framework for your next post.

The biggest mistake beginners make while learning programming?

Trying to learn everything at once.

Python today.
React tomorrow.
Docker next week.
Kubernetes after that.

And somehow, after six months, they still can't build a complete project.

Here's a better approach:

1. Pick one language.
2. Understand the fundamentals.
3. Build a small project.
4. Break it.
5. Fix it.
6. Repeat.

Depth before breadth.

Your first working project teaches more than 20 unfinished tutorials.

Nobody talks enough about the boring side of being a content creator.

Writing when you have no ideas.
Editing when you're tired.
Researching when a topic seems confusing.
Posting when your last post got 12 likes.

The internet shows you viral moments.
It rarely shows you the 100 posts that came before them.

Consistency isn't glamorous.
But it's what builds the foundation.

Keep creating.

3 lessons I learned after experimenting with automation:

1. Automate repetitive tasks, not broken processes.

2. Human approval is important when an action has real consequences.

3. Always build error handling. The happy path isn't the only path.

Automation isn't just connecting APIs and adding AI.
It's designing reliable workflows.

A good automation saves time.
A great automation also prevents mistakes.

What's one task you wish you could automate?

Hot take: Not every business needs an AI agent.

Sometimes a simple Python script is enough.
Sometimes an API integration solves the problem.
Sometimes a traditional rule-based workflow is more reliable.

We should stop adding AI just because it's trending.

Start with the problem.
Understand the workflow.
Choose the simplest technology that solves it.

Technology should serve the problem, not the other way around.

Want to grow on LinkedIn without posting motivational quotes every day?

Try these 5 content ideas:

Monday: Share a lesson from something you learned.
Tuesday: Explain a tool or concept.
Wednesday: Share an unpopular opinion.
Thursday: Break down a real-world problem.
Friday: Share resources that helped you.

You don't need to be an expert in everything.

You just need to share useful things with the people one step behind you.

Consistency + usefulness = a strong starting point.

I don't think college teaches you everything you need for the tech industry.

And that's okay.

College gives you foundations.
Projects give you practical experience.
Internships expose you to real workflows.
Communities help you learn from others.

Your learning doesn't end with a degree.

The best developers I know are still learning something new every week.

Stay curious. Stay humble. Keep building.

A thread on why most AI projects never make it to production:

1. The team focuses on the model instead of the actual user problem.

2. There is no evaluation strategy.

3. Nobody considers latency and cost.

4. The system has no fallback when the model fails.

5. Security and data privacy are treated as afterthoughts.

A successful AI product is much more than a clever prompt.

It's an entire engineering system.

Building a demo is easy. Building something reliable is the real challenge.

Your content doesn't need to go viral to be successful.

Imagine this:

Your post reaches 300 people.
50 people genuinely read it.
10 people learn something useful.
2 people start a conversation with you.

That might be more valuable than 100K random impressions.

Stop judging every post by likes alone.

Measure conversations, trust, and opportunities too.

Things I wish I knew before starting with Generative AI:

- Prompt engineering is useful, but context engineering matters too.
- RAG doesn't automatically guarantee accurate answers.
- More chunks don't always mean better retrieval.
- LLM outputs need validation.
- Model selection should consider cost, latency, and quality.
- Evaluation is not optional.

The real challenge isn't making an LLM respond.
It's making it respond reliably.

What was your biggest learning while building with LLMs?

A reminder for every creator who feels stuck:

Your first 10 posts might be average.
Your first 20 videos might get very few views.
Your first 30 ideas might not work.

That's not failure.
That's feedback.

Every post improves your ability to communicate.
Every experiment teaches you about your audience.
Every mistake makes the next attempt better.

Don't wait until you're perfect to start creating.

Create, learn, improve, repeat.
